title: No BNFC tonight
topic: Working beyond competence and asking for help
stem:
You are an F2 doctor covering paediatrics overnight. A nurse asks you to prescribe IV phenytoin for a child who has had a prolonged seizure, as the registrar has asked. You have never prescribed it for a child.

The hospital IT system is down, so you can't access the online children's formulary.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Calculate the dose from the adult dose, adjusted for weight.
options.brief: Adult doses don't scale reliably for children.
options.detailed: Children's doses often differ from simple weight-adjusted adult doses, and phenytoin has a narrow therapeutic range.

options.text: Ask the paediatric registrar to confirm the dose.
options.brief: The registrar asked for it and can confirm the dose.
options.detailed: The registrar decided on the drug and can confirm the dose and how to give it. Asking is quick and safe.

options.text: Ask the nurse what dose is usually given.
options.brief: Useful as a check, but not a reliable source on its own.
options.detailed: Experienced nurses often know usual doses, which makes this tempting, but the prescriber is responsible, and the dose needs a reliable source.

options.text: Wait until the IT system is back before prescribing.
options.detailed: The seizure needs treatment, and other reliable sources are available.

options.text: Search for the dose using a general internet search on your phone.
options.brief: Online sources may not be reliable.
options.detailed: Some websites are reliable, but an unverified search isn't a safe basis for a paediatric dose of phenytoin.

options.text: Check a printed copy of the children's formulary on the ward.
options.brief: Wards usually keep printed copies for this situation.
options.detailed: Many wards keep printed copies of the BNF for Children or local guidelines. Checking it gives you a reliable source.

options.text: Ask the on-call pharmacist for advice.
options.brief: Pharmacists can advise on paediatric dosing.
options.detailed: The on-call pharmacist can confirm the dose and preparation, especially for a drug with specific administration requirements.

options.text: Prescribe the dose you remember from your medical school notes.
options.brief: Memory isn't reliable for an unfamiliar paediatric dose.
options.detailed: Relying on memory for an unfamiliar drug in a child risks a serious error.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you prescribe an unfamiliar drug safely when your usual source isn't available.
explanation.keyDetails: The child needs treatment now. Phenytoin has a narrow therapeutic range. You haven't prescribed it for a child before.
explanation.reasoning: [B], [F] and [G] all use reliable sources of advice. The distractors use unreliable methods ([A], [C], [E], [H]), or delay treatment ([D]).
explanation.competing: [C] is tempting because nurses often know usual doses, but as prescriber you need a reliable source.

references.title: Good practice in proposing, prescribing, providing and managing medicines and devices
references.note: Prescribing only when you have enough knowledge of the medicine and the patient.
